stories.headline: 'India-Russia ties an 'added value', can help end war'
stories.title: 'India-Russia ties an 'added value', can help end war'
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: New Delhi: The Netherlands sees India's continued engagement with Russia as an "added value," as it believes New Delhi can use its ties with Moscow to persuade it to end the Ukraine war, Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen said on Sunday.
Berendsen is on an official visit to India from November 22 to 23.
He co-chaired the inaugural Foreign Ministers' Meeting with External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar in New Delhi on Sunday and reviewed the India-Netherlands Strategic Partnership.

"We understand that India has its own history, its own role in the world and its own relations," Berendsen told PTI, responding to a question on India's strategic autonomy and its continued engagement with Moscow.

"We actually see it as an added value of our relationship with India that it has a relationship with Russia and can also use that relation to show Russia that it needs to put an end to this war and accept a ceasefire," he said.
The Russia-Ukraine war, in its fifth year, continues with intensified attacks from both sides.
Russia has stepped up strikes on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure, while US-brokered peace talks have made little progress beyond a prisoner swap.

Berendsen said India and the Netherlands, as trading countries, shared concerns over maritime security and freedom of navigation, and needed to work together to address challenges in an increasingly uncertain world.
"I think we're dealing with the same challenges: how to decrease dependencies, how to be more strategically autonomous on critical raw materials, technology and energy," he said.
"If you want to do that, you need to diversify, which means new partnerships.
I think the Netherlands, the EU and India are doing exactly that," he added.
On trade, he described the proposed India-European Union free trade agreement, expected to be signed in December, as a crucial step that could open opportunities beyond merchandise trade.

stories.headline: BJD accuses Odisha govt of using foreign visit probe to divert attention from flood crisis
stories.title: BJD accuses Odisha govt of using foreign visit probe to divert attention from flood crisis
stories.summary: BJD leaders accused the Odisha government of using an inquiry into Naveen Patnaik's foreign visits to divert attention from flood management failures and other governance issues.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: BJD leaders accused the Odisha government of using an inquiry into Naveen Patnaik's foreign visits to divert attention from flood management failures and other governance issues.

Bhubaneswar: The Opposition Biju Janata Dal (BJD) has targeted the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led Odisha government, alleging that the inquiry into alleged irregularities in the foreign visits of former Chief Minister Naveen Patnaik and others during the previous state government was ordered to divert public attention from the principal opposition party's criticism of the current state government over the recent devastating floods across the state.

Addressing a press conference in Bhubaneswar on Sunday, BJD MLA and party's general secretary Goutam Buddha Das and spokesperson Lenin Mohanty said the party welcomed the inquiry into the foreign visits of former Chief Minister Naveen Patnaik and his close aide and the then Private Secretary to Patnaik, V.K. Pandian.
Das alleged that the Odisha government is using the issue to divert attention from the double-engine government's failures in disaster management, law and order and pension distribution.
He said the state government has rejected a proposal by the BJD for a discussion in the Odisha Assembly on the devastating floods in Ganjam district, fearing that its shortcomings would be exposed.
"The Government is nervous that people will come to know the truth.
The Double-Engine Government has failed in several areas, including law and order, distribution of social security pensions and flood management.
To divert public attention from its failures, the state government has brought up an irrelevant issue in the form of an inquiry," Das added.
The senior BJD leader alleged that previous inquiries ordered into three issues targeting the regional party and its leaders have also failed to establish any wrongdoing.
Referring to the Jagannath Temple's Ratna Bhandar controversy, Das said that BJP leaders had alleged before the elections that its valuables were looted and taken to Tamil Nadu.
However, the state government later confirmed that all valuables are safe.
The BJD leader also cited the allegations over Pandian's helicopter visits, saying the inquiry and subsequent court proceedings has given him a clean chit.

stories.headline: India, China hold 10-day talks to ease LAC tensions in Arunachal Pradesh
stories.title: India, China hold 10-day talks to ease LAC tensions in Arunachal Pradesh
stories.summary: The talks focused on establishing engagement protocols, preventing face-offs and misunderstandings between troops deployed along the frontier, and maintaining open communication channels
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: India and China have concluded a second round of Corps Commander-level talks aimed at easing tensions along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in Arunachal Pradesh and putting in place measures to prevent friction between troops deployed along the frontier ahead of the onset of harsh winter conditions.
Sources in the Ministry of Defence confirmed that the closely guarded discussions, which began on November 8, 2026, a day after Deepavali, continued for nearly 10 days, with a short break in between.
The talks were described as cordial, though it remains unclear whether the measures discussed will be implemented on the ground before winter sets in fully.
Lieutenant-General Girish Kalia, General Officer Commanding of the Army’s III Corps, also known as the Spear Corps, led the Indian delegation.
The formation is headquartered at Rangapahar near Dimapur in Nagaland.
His Chinese counterpart and other military officers participated in the discussions.
An official from the Ministry of External Affairs was also present.

The latest round of talks primarily focused on establishing engagement protocols between the two sides, preventing face-offs and misunderstandings between troops deployed along the frontier, maintaining open communication channels and reducing tensions in the eastern sector.
Both countries have deployed substantial numbers of troops in the region.

The discussions assume significance as winter conditions along the LAC in Arunachal Pradesh can become extremely severe, posing considerable challenges to troop sustenance, movement and logistical support.
Any delay in implementing the measures discussed could complicate the situation on the ground as temperatures fall and access to forward areas becomes increasingly difficult.
The second round follows the first Corps Commander-level meeting, held on September 6 and 7, 2026, at the Wacha-Damai Border Personnel Meeting (BPM) point in the Kibithoo sector.

stories.headline: The Decade India Turned the Tide on Poverty
stories.title: The Decade India Turned the Tide on Poverty
stories.summary: A year ago, during my visit to Kiphire, an aspirational district in the remote hills of Nagaland, I interacted with tribal women from local self-help groups. Among them was Esther, a Lakhpati Didi, who proudly spoke of her millet-based products reaching customers online, far beyond Nagaland. What stayed with me was their confidence in a better future. I encouraged them to dream bigger and become Crorepati Didis. Their stories reflected a transformation reaching India's remotest corners, where geographical and economic challenges have long constrained opportunities, yet aspirations for a better tomorrow are growing. When the World Bank released its Poverty & Equity Brief on India last month, my interaction in Kiphire came back to me. The report showed that nearly 50 crore Indians had moved out of poverty between 2011 and 2023, while extreme poverty has been almost eradicated. These figures captured the transformation I had witnessed firsthand. It was not always so. For over six decades after Independence, eradicating mass poverty remained an unfulfilled promise. Even in the early 2010s, India was portrayed abroad as a home of enduring destitution, lagging in sanitation, nutrition, clean cooking fuel and banking. The prevailing prescription was simply to put money into the hands of the poor, and poverty would take care of itself. The last decade has overturned that belief. Under PM Narendra Modi's leadership, India has witnessed a fundamental shift from temporary relief to removing the barriers that perpetuate poverty. Guided by Antyodaya, the welfare of the last person in the line, our Government chose the harder path of addressing deprivations, household by household, ensuring development reached those who needed it most. Targeted, Focused and Tailored Garibi is not merely a shortage of income or wages. A household without a secure roof, safe water, sanitation or healthcare remains vulnerable even when its income rises. One illness can wipe out savings and push a family back into poverty. Our Government, therefore, made every intervention targeted at those who needed it, focused on measurable outcomes and tailored to the deprivation it was meant to remove. There was no magic wand. Each scheme required careful identification of beneficiaries, effective delivery and follow-up until the last household was reached. PM Modi has personally and painstakingly monitored implementation, intervened at critical junctures to resolve bottlenecks, ensured follow-ups and encouraged the use of technology to track delivery. This sustained attention has helped translate policy into tangible improvements in people's lives. Health and Dignity Begin at Home A family cannot climb out of poverty while illness and the daily burden of fetching water keep pulling it back. Under Swachh Bharat, access to household toilets has improved sanitation and helped avert an estimated 60,000-70,000 infant deaths a year. Jal Jeevan Mission has expanded rural tap-water connections from about 3 crore households in 2019 to nearly 16 crore, sparing women and girls the long walk for water and reducing exposure to waterborne diseases. Ujjwala Yojana has enabled cleaner, smokeless kitchens, while PM Awas Yojana has provided the security and dignity of pucca homes. Ayushman Bharat, offering cashless hospital care, has strengthened financial protection against medical expenses. Together, they act as insurance against the shocks that once pushed families back into poverty, while lowering household expenditure and freeing time for work. From a Bank Account to an Enterprise Protection keeps families from slipping back into poverty; to rise further, they need opportunities to earn. For crores of people, that journey began with a bank account. Once, it was accepted that only fifteen paise of every rupee sent from the exchequer reached the intended citizen. Direct Benefit Transfer has changed that. Over 59 crore Jan Dhan accounts enable benefits to reach recipients directly, without middlemen. Technology has made this possible at an unprecedented scale. A bank account also provides a safe place for savings and helps establish a financial record, opening doors to formal credit. For those without property, access to the first loan can be life-changing. Two months ago, during an interaction with MUDRA beneficiaries, I met Sushmita Gharai from West Bengal. She lost her father during the pandemic, and her family's printing business subsequently collapsed. With no land or gold as security, a collateral-free MUDRA loan helped her restart the press. Today, she employs 8 people, twice her initial workforce, and plans to expand into digital printing. What stayed with me was her determination to rebuild and grow. Her story reflects the aspirations of countless young Indians whose ambition exceeds their financial means. Under MUDRA, 60 crore loan accounts have been sanctioned, about two-thirds to women, while PM SVANidhi and PM Vishwakarma support street vendors and traditional artisans. Women have led this transformation. Ten crore rural women participate in SHGs that, through the DAY-NRLM and other programmes, have become platforms for savings, skills, credit and entrepreneurship. Over 3.7 crore women have become Lakhpati Didis, with some going further to become Crorepati Didis. Others, trained as Namo Drone Didis, now provide drone-spraying services to farmers. Women once excluded from economic opportunity are building enterprises and livelihoods of their own. The Sankalp for Viksit Bharat For generations, poverty was treated as something India could manage but never end. What appeared unimaginable a decade ago has now been achieved through years of steady work on the ground. Yet this is no time to rest; the road to Viksit Bharat by 2047 brings its own challenges. The next phase builds on this progress to lift the few people still at the bottom of the ladder out of poverty, while ensuring those who have already risen keep advancing and never slip back. The protection offered via various measures must now be complemented by even wider access to finance, markets and the digital economy. Government is building closer links between academia and industry through employment-linked incentives, internships and apprenticeships, while investment in infrastructure is connecting the country as never before. Opportunity cannot remain the preserve of a few. The Prime Minister has said that Viksit Bharat, like freedom, is a commitment that every Indian must live. Having achieved in ten years what remained unfulfilled for six decades, India can face the next twenty with confidence. With the resolve of 140 crore Indians, Viksit Bharat by 2047 is within our reach, and we together will get there. (The author is the Union Minister of Finance and Corporate Affairs, Govt of India. Courtesy: PIB)

stories.summary: India remains the world's fastest-growing major economy, but rising inflation and an unstable rupee are testing its resilience. With volatile oil prices adding to external pressures, how much room do policymakers have to sustain growth and maintain economic stability?
